units.spoken: RLAIF: AI Feedback in Place of Human Labels
Can a language model label replies in place of people, and how does it get fooled?
This page builds on RL Basics and Aligning Language Models with RL. The terms below are the ones this page keeps using.

1. An agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad.
2. A token is a word or a piece of a word; a language model writes its reply one token at a time.

3. Here the agent is the language model. Here the state is the prompt plus the tokens written so far, and the move is the next token. Here the reward is one number for the whole reply, given when the reply ends.
4. RL, short for reinforcement learning, is learning which moves to make from rewards rather than from labelled answers.
5. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. The policy is the language model being trained to write replies.

units.spoken: The same pipeline, a different labeler

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: What. Picture people reading two summaries of one post and picking the better one. Each pick costs a person's time, so collecting enough picks is slow and costly.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: How. Keep everything else the same and swap only the picker: a strong language model reads the two replies and says which is better.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: Why. When it works, labels arrive on demand at about a tenth of the cost of people's labels, and training runs as it did with people's picks.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: Constitutional AI has a language model check harmful replies against a written list of rules. It swapped people out only for harm labels. Can an AI write every kind of label?

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: The running example is Reddit TL;DR, a set of Reddit posts with a short summary written underneath. A model writes two summaries of one post, and the task is to say which summary is better.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: The cat laptop post and its two summaries follow the labeler from its first pick to its last failure.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. One post, two summaries, and the better one marked. The post says a cat knocked a laptop off a table and cracked the screen, and the owner asks what to do. Summary 1 says what happened and what the owner asks, and it is ticked better. Summary 2 only says someone has a cat and a laptop. The lesson is the gap: a summary that says what happened and what the owner asks is better than one that only names the things in the post.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: Figure 1 shows the running example for RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback: a Reddit post about a cat knocking a laptop off a table, with two summaries underneath. The top box holds the post, and below it sit Summary 1, which says what happened and what the owner asks, and Summary 2, which only says someone has a cat and a laptop, with Summary 1 ticked better. Take the post itself: the summary that says what happened and what the owner asks is the better one, a label an AI can write.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: A reward model is a language model with a one-number output, trained on people's comparisons so the reply they preferred scores higher.

units.section: 1 People are the slow, costly part
units.spoken: RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, trains a language model to earn a score from such a network, trained on people's comparisons of two replies.

sections.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: Section two, Ask a strong language model which is better

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: The AI labeler

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: What. Picture a strong language model handed a post, two summaries, and instructions to say which summary is better. It was not trained for this job; it answers from what it already knows.

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: How. It reads the post and both summaries, then answers "1" or "2". The chance it answers "1" is the label.

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the better summary gets the higher chance, so the chance itself is a label the reward model can learn from.

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: 2.1The labeler favors the first slot

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: Position bias

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: What. Picture the labeler shown the same two summaries twice, once each way round. A labeler with position bias leans toward the same slot across both orders, whatever the two replies say.

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: How. Show each pair both ways and average the two chances, so the lean toward the first slot cancels.

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the averaged label follows the summary, not the slot, and the better summary wins in either order.

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. One method, two labelers. The left column is RLHF: a person reads two summaries and labels them, and the labels train a reward model. The right column is RLAIF: an AI labeler reads the same two summaries and labels them, and the labels train the same reward model. Both feed the same language model. The lesson is the swap: the method stays the same, only the labeler changes.

units.section: 2 Ask a strong language model which is better
units.spoken: Figure 2 shows the RLHF and RLAIF pipelines side by side, the same method with a different labeler. The left column runs through a person and the right column through an AI labeler. Take the cat laptop pair: a person would read both summaries and pick one, and the AI labeler does the same job by answering "1" or "2".
Section three, Labels from probabilities
3.1One label from both orders
The soft label

What. Picture the labeler answering "1" or "2" not with a hard pick but with a chance for each choice. That chance is the soft label: a number between zero and one that says how strongly the labeler leans.
How. Ask the pair both ways round, take the chance for Summary 1 from each order, and average the two.
Why. When it works, a pair the labeler finds close moves the two scores apart only a little, and a clear pair moves them far apart.

Here the reward model is trained with a cross-entropy loss on the softmax of its scores: softmax turns scores into chances that add to one, and the loss penalizes chances that miss the soft label, so the scores match the soft label instead of a hard yes or no.
Equation 1. The both-order soft label. Take the cat laptop pair: Summary 1 is better, but in one order it sits first and in the other it sits second.
Take a look at this equation. Two orders become one soft label: the chance for Summary 1 from each order, averaged so the order stops mattering.

The first-order line. Pee sub 1 is the soft label for Summary 1, one number between zero and one. The half is the first half of the average, half of this order's chance now. Pee sub A I of "1" given ex, why sub 1, why sub 2 is the labeler's chance of answering "1" with Summary 1 first. Ex is the cat laptop post. Why sub 1 is Summary 1, and why sub 2 is Summary 2. The quoted "1" names the first-slot summary, and the bar reads given. Intuitively, this line holds only the first order, half of one chance, with the bracket still open.
Intuition. This line holds only the first order: half of one chance, with the bracket still open.
Example. Take the cat laptop pair with Summary 1 first: the labeler names Summary 1 by answering "1", and this chance is the first half of the average.

The second-order line. The plus adds a second chance to the first line's chance. Pee sub A I of "2" given ex, why sub 2, why sub 1 is the labeler's chance of answering "2" with the order swapped. Why sub 2 now sits in the first slot, and why sub 1 sits in the second slot. The bar again reads given, and ex is the same post. With the bracket closed, the half scales the sum of the two chances, one per order. Intuitively, the second order names the same summary from the other slot, so the order stops mattering.
Intuition. The second order names the same summary from the other slot, so the order stops mattering.
Example. Take the cat laptop pair shown Summary 2 first: the labeler leans toward answering "2", naming Summary 1 again, so the average of the two chances follows Summary 1 and not the slot.
So the soft label averages the two chances for Summary 1, one per order, so the order stops mattering.
The average cancels the position bias. A tie gives one half.
3.2Skipping the reward model
Direct RLAIF
What. Picture the labeler rating each fresh summary the policy writes, on the spot, instead of first training a separate scorer. The rating is the reward itself.
How. Ask the labeler for a rating from 1 to 10 and take its expected rating, each rating weighted by how likely the labeler is to give it.
Why. When it works, the scores stay fresh as the policy's summaries drift, because no trained scorer sits between the labeler and the reward.
SFT, supervised fine-tuning, trains the model on replies people wrote with the ordinary next-token loss; RL usually starts from that model.
For summaries, the SFT model is trained on Reddit posts and the summaries people wrote.
An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is.
The labeler's expected rating, once normalized, is the reward. The scorer it skips is the reward model trained on those soft labels.
The reference model is a frozen copy of the SFT model, a copy that never changes during training.

KL measures how different two probability distributions are, zero when they match; the KL penalty charges the policy for drifting away from the reference model. The paper uses beta 0.05. Raising beta holds the policy closer to the reference model, and lowering beta lets the reward pull it further away. Beta also scales the reward down by one minus beta.

Equation 2. The direct RLAIF score before normalization. A reward model takes a second training run, and its scores go stale as the policy's summaries drift. Take the cat laptop pair: the labeler rates each fresh summary on the spot, and that rating is the score.
Take a look at this equation. The labeler's average rating for one fresh summary is the score, before normalization.

The direct score line. Ar sub A I is the score before normalization, one number for one fresh summary. The sum adds one term per rating, with vee running from 1 to 10. Each term multiplies the rating vee by pee sub A I of vee given ex and why, the labeler's chance of writing that rating. Ex is the cat laptop post, and why is one fresh summary the policy wrote. A likely rating counts more, and an unlikely one counts less. Intuitively, skipping the reward model means asking the labeler to score each fresh summary on the spot.
Intuition. Skipping the reward model means asking the labeler to score each fresh summary on the spot, and the score is its average rating.
Example. Take a fresh summary that says what the owner asks: the labeler puts most of its chance on the highest ratings, so the sum sits near the top.
So the score for one fresh summary is the labeler's average rating for it, each rating weighted by how likely the labeler is to give it.

Take one fresh summary of the cat laptop post that reads smoothly but leaves out what the owner asks. The labeler puts little chance on the highest ratings and most of its chance on the middle ratings, so the sum is pulled toward the middle and the score sits below the score of a summary that says what the owner asks.
The RLAIF paper normalizes that score to run from minus one to one.
3.3How often the AI labeler agrees with people
AI labeler alignment
What. Picture checking the labeler against people: take pairs people already labeled and see how often the labeler picks the same summary. That share is AI labeler alignment.
How. Count how often the labeler picks the same summary people picked, over the labelled pairs.
Why. When it works, a high share means the labeler's picks line up with people's, and a low share means its labels are not worth training on.
The labeler's prompt can carry a few worked example labels, called few-shot examples, or none at all, called zero examples, meaning no worked examples are given.

The downsampled preference set is the labelled pairs the paper kept from the training splits, the data splits used for training, cut down to three to four thousand pairs per task. The labeler is checked on those pairs.
Equation 3. Agreement with people. An AI labeler is only useful if its picks line up with people's picks, so the labeler is checked on pairs people already labeled.
Take a look at this equation. Agreement is the share of labelled pairs where the labeler and the person pick the same summary.

The agreement line. Agreement is that share, one number between zero and one. E, the expectation, takes the average over the labelled pairs in dee. The big bracket holds what is averaged: one marker per pair. The indicator 1 is a marker that is 1 for a matching pair and 0 otherwise. Double-you hat equals double-you is that comparison: double-you is the summary the person picked, and double-you hat is the summary the AI labeler picked. Each pair gives 1 when the picks match and 0 when they differ. Intuitively, the check needs pairs people already labeled, so each of the labeler's picks can be scored against the person's pick.
Intuition. The check needs pairs people already labeled, so each of the labeler's picks can be scored against the person's pick.
Example. Take the cat laptop pair: the person and the labeler both pick Summary 1, so the marker is 1.
So agreement is that share of labelled pairs where the labeler and the person pick the same summary.

Take the labelled pairs the labeler was checked on, with the cat laptop pair among them. Where the labeler and the person both pick Summary 1, the marker is 1; where they split, the marker is 0. Adding the markers over all the pairs and dividing by the number of pairs gives the share where the two picks agree.
The paper calls this share zee sub A C C: the share of the labelled pairs where the labeler and the person pick the same summary.

sections.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update

units.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update
units.spoken: Section four, From both-order labels to an RL update

units.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. From a post and two summaries to an RL update. It starts at the top with the post and two summaries the SFT model wrote. The AI labeler reads the instructions, the post, and both summaries, and its chances become a soft label. The order swaps, the labeler is asked again, and the two soft labels average into one, so the position bias cancels. A reward model trains on those labels and puts a score bar on each summary. Below that, the SFT model, the starting policy, writes fresh summaries, and the reward model scores each finished one. The return pushes each token, with a KL charge against the SFT model, and the value model guesses the score the finished reply usually gets. The lesson is the chain: label, average, train the scorer, then run RL on fresh summaries.

units.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update
units.spoken: Figure 3 shows the whole pipeline as one chain. The labeler writes its reasoning first, called chain of thought, then its chances become a soft label. The order swaps, and the two soft labels average into one. A reward model trains on those labels. The SFT model writes fresh summaries for the reward model to score. Each fresh summary is one reply, one episode. The return, all the reward still to come, pushes each token. The value model guesses the score the finished reply usually gets and starts from the SFT model.

units.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update
units.spoken: The RL step, for both the RLHF and the RLAIF policies, is REINFORCE with a baseline, not proximal policy optimization, which makes small updates so one batch cannot wreck the policy. The value model guesses the score at each token, and the update pushes each token up or down by how much the final reward beat that guess.

units.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update
units.spoken: The RL run used batches of 128 replies, a learning rate of 1e-5, 8 passes over the data, sampling at temperature 0.9, and beta 0.05. Higher temperature means more varied replies, lower temperature steadier ones. Higher learning rates move the policy faster but can overshoot; lower ones move it slower. Larger batches steady the update; more passes reuse the data. Training holds the policy, the value model and the reward model in memory at once; direct RLAIF swaps the reward model for the labeler.

units.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update
units.spoken: PaLM 2 is the family of large language models used for labelling here: L is the large size, S is small, and XS is extra small. A checkpoint is a saved copy of a model. The run behind this page worked on three tasks: Reddit TL;DR summaries, helpful dialogue, where the model answers a person's question, and harmless dialogue, where the safer reply wins. Its policy is PaLM 2 XS, and the policy and value model start from the SFT model. Its reward models start from PaLM 2 XS checkpoints, except the reward model for summaries, which starts from the SFT model. The main labels come from PaLM 2 L, every pair asked in both orders and averaged, and the direct RLAIF labeler is a PaLM 2 XS further trained to follow instructions.

units.section: 4 From both-order labels to an RL update
units.spoken: Take a look at this walkthrough. It follows the cat laptop pair through the same pipeline, one stage at a time, eleven stages in all. The post and two summaries come in, the SFT model wrote both, and the AI labeler reads them. Stage 3 lights the first line of the soft-label card, and stage 5 lights both lines, once the order has swapped and the two chances have averaged. Then the reward model trains, the starting policy writes fresh summaries, and the RL step scores each one. The lesson is the walk: each stage lights up the part of the pipeline it uses.

Section five, Both-order labels and direct scores
The code below reads the cat laptop post and its two summaries: the "1" vs "2" probabilities, the both-order label, and the direct reward.

The labeler function takes the prompt and returns the AI labeler's next-token logits, the model's raw scores for each next token before they are turned into probabilities; I D sub 1 and I D sub 2 are the token ids of "1" and "2".

This code is the both-order soft label and the direct RLAIF reward, in torch. The first function reads the "1" vs "2" probabilities: it takes the labeler's raw scores for the next token, picks the scores for "1" and "2", and turns them into chances that add to one. The second function builds the both-order soft label: it asks the labeler with Summary 1 first and takes the chance of "1", then asks again with the order swapped and takes the chance of "2", and averages the two. The third function builds the direct RLAIF reward: it takes the labeler's chances over the ratings from 1 to 10, multiplies each rating by its chance and adds them up for the expected rating, then scales it to run from minus one to one. The lesson is the shape: probabilities in, one averaged label or one scaled score out.
1. Reads the "1" vs "2" probabilities.
2. The both-order soft label card: both orders read and averaged.
3. The direct RLAIF score card: the expected rating, scaled to run from minus one to one.

sections.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: Section six, How labeler size and order change agreement

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. Sixty simulated pairs, with a bar for the share that agrees with people. Each dot is one simulated pair, placed by which summary the labeler leans toward. A ring shows which summary the person picked, filled when the labeler agrees and hollow when it disagrees, and a dashed trail marks a pick that flipped when the order swapped. The bar shows the share where the labeler agrees with people. The lesson is the pattern: most dots sit on the agreeing side, and the flipped ones carry trails.

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: Figure 4 shows one labeler judging sixty simulated pairs. Each dot is one simulated pair, placed by which summary the labeler leans toward, and the bar shows the share where the labeler agrees with people; a dashed trail marks a pick that flipped when the order swapped. Take one flipped pick: the labeler leans one way with Summary 1 first and the other way when the order swaps.

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: Take a look at this tool. Both orders cut the flips, and a larger labeler agrees with people more often. Sixty simulated pairs sit on the board, and two controls shape them: the labeler size, extra small, small or large, and the order, one order or both orders averaged. The order swaps six times, then the dots stop moving, with a trail on every pick that flipped. The lesson is the comparison: a larger labeler and both orders together fill the agreement bar furthest.

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: Try the tool. Move the size slider from extra small to large and watch the bar grow and the trails thin out. Then switch from one order to both orders averaged and watch the flipped picks settle and the bar fill further. Take the large labeler with both orders averaged: the bar fills to about four fifths. The lesson is the two levers: size and both orders each lift agreement, and together they lift it most.

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: The bar grows when the labeler gets larger or when both orders are averaged. Take the large labeler with both orders averaged: the bar fills to about four fifths, while the extra small labeler with one order fills little more than half. The paper measured a similar climb: large 78.0, small 73.8, extra small 62.7 in percent agreement.

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. Both orders averaged, so no pick flips. A fresh draw of simulated pairs, each dot now sitting at its averaged lean. The dashed trails are gone because no pick flips, and the bar fills further than in one order. The lesson is the average: averaging the two orders steadies each dot and lifts agreement.

units.section: 6 How labeler size and order change agreement
units.spoken: Figure 5 shows a fresh draw of simulated pairs with both orders averaged. Each dot now sits at its averaged lean, the dashed trails are gone because no pick flips, and the bar fills further than in one order. Take a pair that flipped before: its dot now sits between its two one-order places, and no trail marks it.
Section seven, The AI labeler's settings
Two settings shape the labels: the labeler's size, whether it reasons before it picks.
The AI labeler plugs into the loop in two places: up front, it labels pairs to train the reward model, or during RL, it rates each reply the policy writes.

This table lists the settings, and what changing each one does. Read across a row to see one setting and its value, and down the Raise and Lower columns to compare the trade-offs. AI labeler size is PaLM 2 L for the main labels, with small and extra small also tested. Raising it, the labeler agrees with people more and its position bias weakens: 18 in 100 pick the same slot, and 94 in 100 of those pick the first slot. Lowering it is cheaper, but the position bias strengthens: 21 in 100 pick the same slot at small size and 56 in 100 at extra small size, and of those, 91 in 100 at small size and 99 in 100 at extra small size pick the second slot. Reasoning before the pick is used for the main summary labels, with the best prompt being detailed instructions plus chain of thought, reasoning before the pick, and zero examples; few-shot examples helped only on some tasks. Raising it gives a small, consistent gain on summaries, while lowering it gives shorter, cheaper prompts. The lesson is the trade-off: a larger labeler and reasoning before the pick both cost more, and both buy agreement.
The direction depends on size: the large labeler leans toward the first slot, while the small and extra small labelers lean toward the second.
The Constitutional AI repository publishes the prompts and principles from the original RLAIF paper.

sections.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: Section eight, When an AI labeler is good enough

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: The run that answers this question trained the same three tasks twice, once with human labels and once with AI labels, the same way otherwise, and compared the finished models by asking people which replies they preferred. Separately, the labeler's agreement with people, called zee sub A C C, was measured on the labelled pairs of the downsampled preference set.

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: On summaries the AI-labelled model won 71 in a hundred over SFT, against 73 for the human-labelled one, and on helpful dialogue 63 against 64. Head to head, about even at 50 on summaries and 52 on helpful dialogue. On harmless dialogue it did better: 88 in every 100 replies judged harmless, against 76 for the human-labelled model and 64 for SFT, a gap too large to be chance, which the paper calls statistically significant. Judging a reply is just asking the model a question, so the same model that writes replies can judge them. On summaries, RLAIF with a labeler the size of the policy was preferred 68 times in a hundred over the SFT model; on helpful dialogue, direct RLAIF with the model labelling its own training was preferred 66 times in a hundred. Direct RLAIF beat same-size RLAIF on summaries, 74 in a hundred over SFT and 60 head to head. The AI reward model agreed with people 74.2 times in a hundred, against 79.3 for the human-labelled one, yet the finished models matched.

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: Share of replies judged harmless.

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: 1. You have a strong language model but few labels. The labeler writes labels on demand at about a tenth of the cost of human labels, but it must be strong: small labelers agree with people much less, as the size slider shows.

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: 2. The labeler can read both candidates. The label comes from comparing two replies side by side, so a task where the labeler cannot see both replies at once does not fit this shape.

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: 3. The reward model is trained once up front and stays fixed during RL, so labels go stale as the policy's replies drift. Fresh labels from the labeler, or direct rating during RL, keep them current.

units.section: 8 When an AI labeler is good enough
units.spoken: Those three points fit the cat laptop post: a strong model but few labels can label its summaries, and the labeler reads both summaries.

sections.section: 9 How an AI labeler gets fooled

units.section: 9 How an AI labeler gets fooled
units.spoken: Section nine, How an AI labeler gets fooled

units.section: 9 How an AI labeler gets fooled
units.spoken: This table lists what breaks it, and the fix for each. Read across a row to see one cause, its symptom, and its fix. Position bias makes the label flip with the order, so average both orders. A small labeler agrees with people much less, even after averaging, so use a larger labeler. Longer replies run longer than the SFT replies, which can tip human judges toward the longer reply, so compare at equal length. Direct RLAIF needs a labeler call per reply, so the labeler rates each fresh summary and RL runs slowly, so use a smaller labeler for rating. The lesson is the guard: average the orders, size the labeler to the job, and compare at equal length.

units.section: 9 How an AI labeler gets fooled
units.spoken: Comparing at equal length means judging replies of the same length. The paper found real failures: the RLHF-trained policy's summary said the author was 20, though the post never says so, and the AI-labelled summaries sometimes ran on with repeated phrases.

units.section: 10 Learning from AI-labelled pairs without RL
units.spoken: Section ten, Learning from AI-labelled pairs without RL

units.section: 10 Learning from AI-labelled pairs without RL
units.spoken: Do we even need a reward model and an RL loop to learn from these pairs?

units.section: 10 Learning from AI-labelled pairs without RL
units.spoken: The cat laptop pair is a preference pair: one post, two summaries, a label saying which reply is better. Direct preference optimization (DPO) turns one pair into an update by raising the chance of the preferred reply and lowering the chance of the other, with no reward model and no RL loop.

units.section: 10 Learning from AI-labelled pairs without RL
units.spoken: Group relative policy optimization (GRPO) works on groups of answers, and DeepSeek-R1 replaces the labeler with a program where answers can be checked. GRPO writes a group of answers to one prompt, scores each one, and pushes the policy toward the answers above the group average. DeepSeek-R1 is the reasoning model trained that way: it answers maths and code questions, and a program checks each answer, so no labeler scores it.
